slides.title: Day, night and the seasons
bullets: Day and night: Earth rotates once every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the side facing away has night.
Sunrise is always in the east; sunset is always in the west.
Seasons: Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5°. As Earth orbits the Sun, each hemisphere tilts towards or away.
When the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun → summer. Tilts away → winter.

slides.title: What do you think about the Moon?
bullets: The Moon is always in the sky — it can be seen during the day as well as at night.
The Moon does not produce its own light — it reflects sunlight.
The Moon orbits Earth once every 27–29 days, causing the phases.
The phases are not caused by Earth's shadow — they are caused by which part of the lit Moon we can see.

slides.title: Moon phases and lunar eclipses
bullets: New Moon → Crescent → Half (First Quarter) → Gibbous → Full Moon → Gibbous → Half (Third Quarter) → Crescent → New Moon.
A lunar eclipse happens when Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow on the Moon.
Lunar eclipses only happen at full Moon.
The Moon is always present — we just can't always see it clearly.

slides.title: Relative clauses in action
bullets: A relative clause adds information about a noun: 'Saturn, which has rings made of ice and rock, is the sixth planet from the Sun.'

Without the relative clause the sentence still makes sense: 'Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun.'

slides.title: Three ways to use parenthesis
bullets: Brackets: 'Mars (the fourth planet from the Sun) is roughly half the size of Earth.'
Dashes: 'Neptune — the furthest planet from the Sun — takes 165 Earth years to complete one orbit.'
Commas: 'Venus, the hottest planet in our solar system, has a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide.'
All three add extra information — the main sentence must still make sense if you remove the parenthesis.

slides.title: Our three-paragraph structure

Each paragraph begins with a topic sentence that tells the reader what is coming.

key_facts: The Big Bang began the universe about 13.8 billion years ago.
Our solar system sits inside the Milky Way galaxy.
Eight planets orbit the Sun, from Mercury to Neptune.
The inner planets are rocky; the outer ones are gas giants.
Earth rotates once every 24 hours, causing day and night.
Earth's 23.5° tilt gives us the four seasons as we orbit the Sun.
The Moon orbits Earth every 27–29 days and reflects sunlight.
Planets vary in size, distance from the Sun and temperature.

sort_cards.title: Rocky or Gas Giant? — Sort the Solar System

items.text: Mercury — tiny rocky planet, closest to the Sun, no atmosphere
Venus — rocky planet, thick cloudy atmosphere, hottest planet
Earth — rocky planet, liquid water, the only planet known to support life
Mars — rocky, red surface, thin atmosphere, two small moons
Jupiter — enormous ball of gas, no solid surface, at least 95 moons
Saturn — gas giant, famous rings of ice and rock, lighter than water
Uranus — ice giant, rotates on its side, faint rings
Neptune — ice giant, strongest winds in the solar system, furthest from Sun
The Sun — a star that produces its own heat and light (not a planet)
Pluto — reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 — too small to be a full planet
The Moon — Earth's natural satellite; orbits Earth, not the Sun
Asteroids — rocky objects orbiting the Sun, mostly in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter

columns.heading: which (for things)
items: Saturn, which has rings made of ice and rock, is the sixth planet from the Sun.
The Milky Way, which contains billions of stars, is our home galaxy.
Jupiter, which is eleven times wider than Earth, is the largest planet.
Neptune, which takes 165 years to orbit the Sun, is the furthest planet.

columns.heading: where (for places)
items: The asteroid belt, where millions of rocky objects orbit the Sun, lies between Mars and Jupiter.
The solar system, where eight planets travel around our star, sits inside the Milky Way.
Venus, where temperatures reach 465°C, is the hottest planet.
Mars, where two small moons orbit the planet, has a thin atmosphere.

columns.heading: Brackets ( )
items: Mars (the fourth planet from the Sun) is roughly half the size of Earth.
Jupiter (the largest planet in our solar system) has at least 95 known moons.
The Moon (Earth's only natural satellite) takes 27 days to orbit our planet.
Pluto (once considered the ninth planet) was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

columns.heading: Dashes —
items: Neptune — the furthest planet from the Sun — takes 165 Earth years to complete one orbit.
Saturn's rings — made of ice and rock — stretch up to 282,000 km from the planet.
The Big Bang — the event that began the universe — happened 13.8 billion years ago.
Venus — despite being further from the Sun than Mercury — is the hottest planet.

columns.heading: Commas ,
items: Venus, the hottest planet in our solar system, has a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide.
The Milky Way, our home galaxy, contains between 200 and 400 billion stars.
Jupiter, a gas giant with no solid surface, spins faster than any other planet.
Earth, the only planet known to support life, orbits the Sun once every 365 days.
